catalog_quote: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word. Examples of stress assignment to the root-final syllable are provided for verbs and nouns in (7-8) and (9-10), respectively. In nouns, this stress pattern is a bit obscured as they always surface with the extrametrical nominalizing enclitic =a. On the surface, then, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of nouns bearing the enclitic =a. (7) /ɛ-pi/ → [ɛ.ˈpi] 2.sg.imp-shut.off ‘Shut off!’ ... (9) /janu=a/ → [ɲã.ˈndu.a] spider=nmlz ‘spider’ (10) /tapiʔiɾ=a/ → [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] tapir=nmlz ‘tapir’ However, some suffixes trigger stress shift from the root-final syllable, both in verbs and nouns. For instance, stress remains on the final syllable of the verb root in (11) after circumfixation of the sentential negation nd(a)-…-i, but shifts in (12) after suffixation of -ahim ‘very’. Another suffix that triggers stress shift is -uhu ‘aug’ …

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the root (word-final on verbs, e.g. [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi] 'cut!'); nouns carry an extrametrical nominalizing enclitic =a, so on the surface they look penultimate ([ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] 'tapir'). Certain suffixes (-ahim 'very', -uhu 'augmentative', -ʔi 'diminutive') attract the stress to themselves; the negation circumfix does not. Marçoli 2018 (p.122, for Tenharim/Jiahui/Amondawa) states the same rule: stress always on the last syllable of the root, oxytone words, shifting right only under derivation/compounding.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by dos Santos 2024 (he indicates primary stress only); Marçoli 2018 lists a secondary-stress symbol in his conventions (p. xii) but gives no rule; Marçoli notes that in some compounds each member keeps its own stress (p.124).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-shifting suffixes -ahim, -uhu, -ʔi (dos Santos pp.41-42); Marçoli: a few lexemes where the argumentative-case -a has become the stressed root vowel (paroxytone [a]-final and -pe postposition forms, p.123).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word = root plus affixes/enclitics); described for the living Kawahíva dialects (Juma, Jupaú, Tenharim, Amondawa, Karipuna, Parintintin, Piripkura), NOT from Paranawát data — see the note on which variety.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Kawahíva (Tupi-Kawahib), the dialect complex to which Paranawát belongs, based on the living varieties: Juma (juma1249), Jupaú/Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau (urue1240), Tenharim/Parintintin/Jiahui (pari1258, tenh1241, diah1239), Amondawa (amun1246), Karipuna (kari1317) and Piripkura. Paranawát itself is dormant; dos Santos 2024 (p.15) says it is attested only by wordlists collected by Nimuendajú, and Glottolog's only reference is the Rondon & Faria 1948 wordlist. No Paranawát-specific phonological description exists, so the catalog entry can only be by inheritance from the Kawahíva complex (Rodrigues' 'Tupí-Kawahíb, Tupí do Machado ou Paranawát' subgroup VI), which the reviewer should decide on rather than merge automatically.

sources.note: §3.2.1 (pp.40-41): 'Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word'; nouns surface with an extrametrical nominalizing enclitic =a so stress appears penultimate on the surface; suffixes -ahim 'very', -uhu 'aug', -ʔi 'dim' shift stress rightward onto themselves. On Paranawát specifically (p.15): a dormant variety 'whose existence is attested to by wordlists collected by Curt Nimuendajú' — no Paranawát data in the grammar.
